The result cannot be calculated from these values
Voltage must be greater than zero
Current must be greater than zero
Resistance must be greater than zero
Impedance must be greater than zero
The power values are not valid or not consistent with each other
Power factor must be between 0 and 1 (φ between 0° and 90°)
A value is out of range
Finds the current drawn by a load from two known circuit values: voltage, power, resistance or impedance. In AC, when the result depends on the phase shift, the power factor is also required.
Finds the supply voltage of a load from two circuit values. In three-phase systems the result is the line-to-line voltage.
Calculates active power, the power the load actually turns into work, heat or light. Measured in watts.
Calculates apparent power, voltage times current regardless of the phase shift. It is what transformers, generators and cables are sized for.
Calculates reactive power, which flows back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric fields of the load without being consumed. It only exists in AC.
Calculates the power factor (cos φ) and the phase angle between voltage and current from the known values of the load.
Calculates the resistance of a load: the part of its opposition to current that dissipates energy as heat.
Calculates the AC impedance of a load: its total opposition to current, combining resistance and reactance.
Calculates how much the voltage falls along a line because of the resistance and reactance of its conductors, with the load at the far end. It also gives the voltage that actually reaches the load.
The method follows Annex G of IEC 60364-5-52. Compare the result with the maximum drop allowed by the code that applies to your installation.

DC: current always flows in the same direction (batteries, solar panels, DC power supplies).

Single-phase: one phase and neutral; the typical household supply.

Two-phase: two phases, with or without neutral.

Three-phase: three phases, with or without neutral; the usual supply for motors and industrial installations.
Potential difference that drives current through the circuit.
For single-phase enter the line-to-neutral voltage. For two-phase and three-phase enter the line-to-line voltage.
Amount of electric charge flowing through the conductor each second. Measured in amperes.
Opposition of a material to current; the energy it absorbs becomes heat. In AC it is the real part of the impedance.
Total opposition of a circuit to alternating current. It combines resistance with the reactance of coils and capacitors.
Power of the load. It can be entered as active, apparent or reactive power.
The selected unit tells which power it is: W, kW, MW, HP or CV for active; VA, kVA or MVA for apparent; var, kvar or Mvar for reactive.
Power the load converts into useful work, heat or light. It is what the energy meter records.
Voltage times current, ignoring the phase shift. It shows how much grid capacity the load takes up.
Power exchanged with magnetic fields (motors, transformers) or electric fields (capacitors) without being consumed. It does no work but still loads the conductors.
Ratio of active to apparent power; the cosine of the angle φ between voltage and current. Ranges from 0 to 1.

Typical values when nameplate data is missing: 1 for resistive loads (heaters, kettles); 0.95 to 0.99 for electronics with active correction (computers, good LED drivers); 0.75 to 0.85 for appliances with small motors (fridges, fans). 0.9 covers most cases.
With the selector on the right you can also enter it as sin φ, tan φ or as the angle φ in degrees or radians.
Load supplied at the end of the line.
Enter it as current (A) or as active, apparent or reactive power; the current is then derived from the voltage and power factor.
Cross-sectional area of the conductor, in mm² or AWG/kcmil.
Number of identical conductors (same size, length and material) connected in parallel on each phase. The current is shared among them.
Distance from the supply point to the load, one way.
Conductor metal. Aluminum has higher resistivity than copper, so it needs a larger size for the same drop.
Single-core: each conductor in its own cable. Multi-core: several insulated conductors under one sheath; they sit closer together and reactance is slightly lower.
Temperature the conductor reaches in service. Higher temperature means higher resistance and a larger drop.
Usual values by insulation: 70 °C for PVC; 90 °C for XLPE or EPR; 60, 75 or 90 °C for NEC types depending on their rating (THHN, for example, is rated 90 °C).
Phase shift between voltage and current
mm² sizes: table resistance at 20 °C and reactance at 50 Hz. AWG/kcmil sizes: table resistance at 75 °C and reactance at 60 Hz (NEC chapter 9).
They are filled in when a form opens or the current type changes. Leave them blank to fill nothing.
Electricalc brings together calculators and tables for electrical installations. Every tool is free.
Results are for guidance only. Always check designs against the applicable code and with a licensed professional.

The bottom bar has five destinations: Home (search, recent and favorites), Project (tools by stage), Calculate (by problem), RIC (the 19 standards) and References (tables, diagrams, connectors, conversions and formulas).
Long-press a tool to add it to or remove it from Favorites. You can also use the star inside each calculator. Search understands “RIC 4” and ignores accents.
In each calculator choose the current type and, where offered, which values you know. Tap ⓘ next to a field to see what it means and what to enter.
The top bar opens the formulas and the screen guide. The “RIC N°xx” chips lead to the related standard. The ⋮ menu exports the result to PDF or shares it.
Consumption of each load, all equal (for example, each luminaire on a lighting run).
How many loads are on the line. They are assumed evenly spaced, with the last one at the end.
Distance from the supply point to the last load, one way.
Voltage drop not to be exceeded, as a percentage of the supply voltage or in volts.
Use the limit required by the code for your installation. The app does not suggest one yet.
Calculates the voltage drop at the end of a line feeding several equal loads spread along its length, such as a row of luminaires or outlets.
Calculates the maximum length a line can have so the voltage drop stays within the given value, with the load at the end. Check separately that the conductor has enough current capacity for the load.
Current at the start of the line
With N equal, evenly spaced loads, the drop equals that of the total load placed at (N + 1)/(2N) of the line length.
